objectives: Explain why preventive maintenance reduces cost and downtime
Compare mileage-, time- and engine-hour-based intervals
Describe common inspection requirements
body: [[PM]] (preventive maintenance) is planned service performed before something fails: oil and filters, lubrication, inspections, adjustments. Reactive (corrective) maintenance happens after a failure — usually at a worse time, a worse place and a higher cost.

body.h: Three ways to trigger a PM

head: Trigger
How it works
Best for
rows: Units that idle heavily or run PTO equipment; reefer units

body: Most fleets use whichever comes first — for example, a PM at a mileage limit or a set number of months, whichever occurs first. Intervals are set by the fleet based on manufacturer recommendations, duty cycle and oil analysis; they vary widely between fleets.
Many fleets use tiered PMs. Names differ, but a common pattern is:

tiles.title: PM A
tiles.text: Basic service: oil and filter, lube, safety inspection of brakes, tires, lights.

tiles.title: PM B
tiles.text: PM A plus additional filters (fuel, air), more detailed inspections.

tiles.title: PM C
tiles.text: Comprehensive service: may include fluids like coolant or transmission, valve adjustment — per manufacturer schedule.

body: In the U.S., commercial vehicles require a periodic (annual) inspection, often called the DOT annual inspection, and drivers complete inspection reports ([[DVIR]]) as required by regulations. Trailers need their own inspections. Your safety department tracks compliance; you coordinate getting units inspected on time.

callout.title: PMs are scheduled around freight
callout.text: A PM that pulls a truck off a paying load is expensive. Good coordinators plan PMs when units are already near a shop, at a terminal, or on a home-time break.

body.title: The same belt: found at a PM vs. failed on the road
body.note: Illustrative figures. The part costs the same either way — the difference is everything around the failure.

example.title: Planning around home time
example.text: T-122 is 1,800 miles from its PM B. The driver goes home Friday for 34 hours, near a terminal shop. Instead of waiting until the PM is overdue mid-week, the coordinator schedules the PM for Saturday morning — zero lost load time.

exercise.prompt: Choose the best primary PM trigger for each unit.

items.text: Long-haul sleeper tractor running 2,500 miles/week
items.why: Steady high mileage makes miles the best wear indicator.

items.text: Dry van trailer parked often at a customer yard
items.why: Low, irregular use — time-based ensures it still gets inspected.

items.text: Reefer unit on a refrigerated trailer
items.why: Reefer units run on their own hours regardless of trailer miles.

items.text: Local day cab that idles for hours at ports
items.why: Heavy idling adds engine wear that mileage doesn't capture.

check.q: What does "whichever comes first" mean in a PM schedule?
o: The PM is done at the mileage limit only
The PM is due at the first of the mileage, time or hours limits reached
PMs are only done after failures
check.e: Multiple triggers protect units that run few miles but still age or idle.

check.q: PM intervals are identical for every fleet.
check.e: Intervals depend on manufacturer guidance, duty cycle, and fleet policy.

check.q: How often must each trailer get a periodic (annual) inspection under U.S. rules?
check.e: 49 CFR 396.17 requires a periodic inspection of every commercial motor vehicle, trailers included, at least once every 12 months.

takeaways: PM prevents failures; reactive repairs cost more and happen at bad times.
Triggers: mileage, time, engine hours — often whichever comes first.
PM levels (A/B/C) vary by fleet.
Schedule PMs around freight and home time.
tips: Plan PMs around home time and loads that end near a shop.
Book the PM appointment when you tell dispatch — not after.
mistakes: Waiting until a PM is overdue to start planning it.
Using mileage-only intervals for units that idle for hours every day.

blocks.title: Seasonal maintenance focus (example calendar)
blocks.note: Illustrative for a fleet with cold winters and hot summers. Prepare before the season, not during it.

deep.title: The annual inspection program
blocks: Every tractor and every trailer needs a periodic inspection at least once every 12 months (49 CFR 396.17). It is separate from PM: a unit can be current on oil changes and still be illegal to dispatch. Missing proof of a periodic inspection is one of the most-cited vehicle violations at roadside, and it is entirely a scheduling problem.

head: Question
Answer
Rule
rows: At least once every 12 months, for each power unit and each trailer
Every item on FMCSA's minimum periodic inspection standards: brakes, steering, lights, tires, wheels, coupling devices, frame, suspension, exhaust and more
A qualified inspector: someone who understands the standards and can find defects, by training or experience. The carrier keeps proof of that person's qualifications
Only a qualified brake inspector, for brake inspection, repair, adjustment and service
What proves it on the road?
A copy of the report, or a decal or sticker that links to it, carried on the vehicle
How long is the report kept?

callout.title: How coordinators keep it clean
callout.text: Track the annual due date by unit, trailers included, as its own schedule. Pair each annual with a PM so the unit visits the shop once. Flag units due in the next 30 days every week, and never let a trailer leave the yard on an expired inspection.

exercise.prompt: Trailer TR-540's annual inspection expired yesterday. It is loaded and due out at 15:00. The yard shop has a qualified inspector free at 13:00. What do you do?

options.text: Let it go and book the inspection for next week.
options.why: An expired periodic inspection is a violation the moment the trailer is on the road, and it shows up on the company record.

options.text: Book the 13:00 inspection, tell dispatch the 15:00 departure depends on it passing, and line up a spare trailer in case defects need repair.
options.why: It fixes the compliance gap before dispatch and protects the load in parallel.

options.text: Put a new decal on it and inspect it later.
options.why: A decal without an inspection is a false record. Never do it.

objectives: Use service history to plan maintenance
Prioritize overdue units
Communicate PM needs to dispatch
body: Service history shows what was done, when and at what mileage. It tells you what is coming due, what keeps failing, and what might be covered by warranty.

head: Status
Meaning
Action
rows: Within planning window (e.g., next 2,000 mi / 2 weeks)
Plan with dispatch around loads and home time

callout.title: Overdue inspections are different
callout.text: A late oil change is a cost risk. An expired annual inspection is a compliance issue — a unit may not be permitted to operate until inspected. Check with your safety department.

body: When a unit is overdue, find out why: dispatch couldn't release it, the shop had no capacity, the driver never came in. The fix is different each time.

body.title: This week's PM board (example 50-unit fleet)
body.note: Work the board right to left: overdue first, then due, then plan the due-soon units into next week's loads.

example.title: The PM that kept slipping
example.text: T-109 was overdue by 6,000 miles because dispatch kept giving it long runs. The coordinator reviewed the next week's loads with dispatch, found a delivery near a partner shop Thursday afternoon, and booked the PM for Thursday evening with a promised release by 06:00 Friday.

exercise.prompt: Order these units from highest to lowest PM priority.
items: T-109: PM A overdue by 6,000 miles
T-126: PM B due this week
T-131: PM A due in 1,800 miles

check.q: Why is an expired annual inspection more serious than a late oil change?
o: It is a compliance issue that may prevent the unit from operating
check.e: Periodic inspection is a regulatory requirement. Consult the safety department.

check.q: A tractor is 4,000 miles overdue for PM because dispatch keeps assigning it loads. You:
o: Ground it immediately without telling dispatch
Work with dispatch to find a load that routes near a shop or align with home time, and escalate if needed
check.e: Coordinate first; escalate per procedure if it keeps slipping.

takeaways: Service history reveals what is due, repeats and warranty.
Track statuses: OK, due soon, due, overdue.
Overdue inspections are compliance issues.
Solve the reason a PM is overdue, not just the symptom.
tips: Ask why each overdue unit is overdue — the answer tells you what to fix.
Check annual inspection dates separately from PM intervals.
mistakes: Treating an expired annual inspection like a late oil change.
Letting the same unit slip three weeks in a row without escalating.

blocks.title: Fitting five PMs into one week of loads
blocks.note: Overdue and compliance items first; due-soon units matched to home time and planned stops.

objectives: Interpret the urgency of common warning lights
Explain what a DTC is and what it isn't
Collect useful code information from drivers and telematics
body: Exact symbols vary by manufacturer, but color is a reliable first clue:

tiles.title: Red
tiles.text: Serious — e.g., STOP ENGINE. Driver should stop safely as soon as possible.

tiles.title: Amber / yellow
tiles.text: Attention needed — e.g., CHECK ENGINE, DPF, DEF. Diagnose soon; monitor for change.

tiles.title: Green / blue
tiles.text: Informational — a system is on or active.

body: A [[DTC]] is a code stored by an electronic control module (like the engine [[ECM]]) when it detects a condition outside normal limits. On heavy trucks, codes are often reported using the J1939 standard as an SPN (Suspect Parameter Number — what is affected) and an FMI (Failure Mode Identifier — how it is out of range).

callout.title: A code is a clue, not a diagnosis
callout.text: A DTC tells a technician where to start looking. A code for a sensor reading might be caused by the sensor, wiring, a connector, or the actual system the sensor measures. Never order parts based on a code alone.

ul: Exact code(s) — SPN and FMI, or the full code text
Whether the code is active or inactive (historical)
Lamp status and messages on the dash
Any derate or speed limitation
When it started and what the driver was doing
Telematics snapshot data, if available

body.title: Warning lamp color guide

stops.d: Information — a system is on or active.
Attention — diagnose soon; watch for any change.
Likely derate — get to a safe place; arrange prompt diagnosis.
Serious — stop safely as soon as possible.

body.note: Symbols vary by manufacturer; color is the most reliable first clue. Always ask the driver to read the exact message.

notes.d: The parameter involved. SPN 3251 relates to DPF differential pressure.
The failure mode. FMI 0 means the data is valid but above the normal operating range.
Present now, and it has occurred more than once.
Tells you the urgency the engine computer assigned.

example.title: Telematics alert at 03:00
example.text: Telematics shows T-120 with an active aftertreatment code and an amber lamp. The truck is still at normal speed. Rather than wake the driver, the coordinator checks the code description, sees that it commonly precedes a derate if not addressed, and books a dealer appointment on the route for the morning — then messages the driver the plan.

items.text: Red STOP ENGINE lamp with low oil pressure message
items.why: Red lamp + oil pressure = potential engine damage.

items.text: Amber check engine lamp, no performance change
items.why: Needs attention, no immediate danger reported.

items.text: Green cruise-control indicator on
items.why: A system status indicator.

items.text: Amber DPF lamp, regen requested by the system
items.why: Follow manufacturer/company procedure for regen; escalate if it fails or a derate begins.

check.q: In a J1939 code, what does the FMI describe?
o: How the parameter is failing (e.g., too high, too low, erratic)
check.e: SPN identifies what; FMI identifies the failure mode.

check.q: If a DTC points to a sensor, the sensor is always the failed part.
check.e: Wiring, connectors or the actual system may be the cause. Technicians confirm with testing.

takeaways: Lamp color gives the first read on urgency.
DTCs = SPN (what) + FMI (how), on J1939 systems.
A code is a clue, not a diagnosis.
Collect active/inactive status, lamps, derates and timing.
tips: Ask for the full code (SPN + FMI), not just "a DPF code".
Note whether a code is active or inactive — shops care about the difference.
mistakes: Ordering parts based on a code alone.
Asking a driver to clear codes before a technician has read them.

blocks.title: Common J1939 FMI codes
head: FMI
Meaning
What it often points to
rows: Data valid but above normal range — most severe
A real condition: pressure/temperature too high
Data valid but below normal range — most severe
A real condition: pressure/level too low
Voltage above normal, or shorted to high source
Voltage below normal, or shorted to low source
Current below normal, or open circuit
Mechanical system not responding or out of adjustment
A component isn't doing what it's told
A reported state — read the SPN description
blocks.note: SAE J1939 failure mode identifiers. FMIs 3–6 usually suggest an electrical circuit issue; 0 and 1 usually suggest the measured condition itself is out of range. A technician confirms either way.

deep.title: Triage a fault list
blocks: Telematics rarely sends one tidy code. You get a list: some active, some old, some repeating. The skill is putting them in order before you call anyone. Here is T-412's fault snapshot at 06:40.

ul: Lamp and status first. An active code with a red lamp outranks everything else on the list.
Count the repeats. A code that has come back four times is a real problem, not a glitch.
Look for one cause behind many codes. Several unrelated sensor codes at once often point to low voltage or one bad connector.
Inactive means history. Note it for the next PM; it is not a road call on its own.
Never ask a driver to clear codes. The technician needs them.

exercise.prompt: Sort each line of T-412's snapshot.

items.text: SPN 100 / FMI 1 · oil pressure low · red STOP lamp · active
items.why: Low oil pressure with a red lamp can destroy an engine in minutes. Stop safely, shut down, arrange service.

items.text: SPN 3251 / FMI 0 · DPF pressure high · amber · active, 4 times
items.why: A clogging DPF leads to a derate. Repeats mean a regen or a cleaning is due: book it before it strands the truck.

items.text: SPN 1761 / FMI 18 · DEF level low · amber · active
items.why: Refill DEF at the next stop. Left alone, the engine will limit power.

items.text: SPN 168 / FMI 18 · battery voltage low · inactive, 12 days ago
items.why: One old occurrence. Ask for a battery and charging test at the next PM.

blocks.note: Descriptions are shown in plain words. Exact SPN and FMI definitions come from the SAE J1939 standard and each engine maker's fault guide; the technician confirms.

objectives: Separate symptoms from causes
Read a technician's diagnostic report
Ask the right questions without pretending to be a technician
body: A symptom is what someone observes: low power, noise, a lamp. A cause is what produced it: a clogged filter, a cracked hose, a failed sensor. The same symptom can have many causes.

flow: Cause: failed regens due to faulty sensor

msg.title: Diagnostic report — T-120
msg.text:
Complaint: Derate, amber DPF lamp
Codes: SPN 3251 FMI 0 (active)
Tests: DPF differential pressure high at idle and under load. Forced regen attempted — aborted, outlet temp sensor reading implausible.
Findings: DPF outlet temperature sensor failed. DPF loaded.
Recommendation: Replace sensor, perform parked regen. If pressure remains high, remove DPF for cleaning.
Est.: 3.2 h labor + sensor. ETR: today 17:00 (if regen successful).

ul: What is the confirmed cause versus what is still being tested?
What is the repair plan, and what is plan B if it doesn't work (e.g., "if pressure remains high")?
Are parts in stock? What is the ETR for each scenario?
Is any of this related to prior repairs (possible warranty or repeat failure)?
Is the unit safe to operate after the repair, or are there other findings?

callout.title: Stay in your lane — confidently
callout.text: You don't need to tell a technician how to test a sensor. You do need to understand the plan well enough to spot risks to time, cost and safety.

example.title: The conditional ETR
example.text: The report above gives an ETR of 17:00 if the regen is successful. The coordinator tells dispatch: "ETR 17:00 best case; if the DPF needs cleaning, likely tomorrow afternoon. I'll confirm by 16:00." Dispatch can now plan for both outcomes.

items.text: Truck limited to 5 mph
items.why: An observed effect (derate).

items.text: Cracked charge air cooler hose
items.why: A physical finding that produces symptoms.

items.text: Amber check engine lamp on
items.why: The lamp is an indicator of some condition.

items.text: Failed DPF outlet temperature sensor
items.why: The confirmed faulty component.

check.q: The shop gives an ETR that depends on a test result. The best update to dispatch is:
o: Give the best case, the likely alternative, and when you'll confirm
Wait until everything is certain before saying anything
check.e: Conditional ETRs let dispatch plan for both outcomes.

check.q: Which question is appropriate for a coordinator to ask a technician?
o: "Why don't you just replace the turbo?"
"What's confirmed versus still being tested, and what's plan B?"
check.e: Understanding the plan and contingencies is the coordinator's job.

takeaways: Symptoms are observed; causes are found.
Diagnostic reports: complaint, codes, tests, findings, recommendation, estimate/ETR.
Ask what's confirmed, what's plan B, and what drives the ETR.
Communicate conditional ETRs honestly.
tips: Ask "what's confirmed and what's still being tested?" on every diagnosis call.
Ask for plan B and its ETR up front.
mistakes: Passing a best-case ETR to dispatch as if it were certain.
Arguing with a technician about the diagnosis instead of asking about the plan.

blocks.title: Diagnostic tools compared
blocks.hint: Ask shops which software they have for the engine make — it often decides who can diagnose an aftertreatment problem.

objectives: Trace the exhaust path through the aftertreatment system
Distinguish passive, active and parked regeneration
Coordinate aftertreatment calls intelligently
body: Aftertreatment problems are among the most frequent causes of derates on modern diesel trucks. You don't need to repair them — but knowing the path the exhaust takes lets you ask sharper questions and choose the right vendor.

head: Type
What happens
Coordinator angle
rows: Soot burns off naturally when exhaust is hot — steady highway driving
Long highway runs help; heavy idling and short hauls work against it
The system raises exhaust temperature while driving
The driver may see a regen or HEST lamp — usually normal
The driver or a technician starts a regen while the truck is parked, per manufacturer procedure
Takes time; if requested and ignored, a derate can follow

body.title: DEF facts that matter on the desk

items.l: urea in diesel exhaust fluid (the rest is deionized water)
about where DEF freezes (−11 °C) — tanks and lines are heated
times DEF should go in the fuel tank — contamination is a costly repair

callout.title: Clearing codes isn't a repair
callout.text: A regen or a cleared code can get a truck moving, but if the DPF keeps loading, something upstream is still wrong — a sensor, an injector, an EGR problem, or the duty cycle.

example.title: Winter morning derate
example.text: On a 5 °F morning a driver reports a DEF warning and reduced power right after startup. The coordinator asks whether the DEF gauge shows fluid (yes, half tank) and how long the truck has been running (ten minutes). Knowing DEF systems are heated and may need time to thaw, the coordinator checks the manufacturer guidance with the shop, which advises letting the system warm up while monitoring. The lamp clears after 25 minutes — no tow needed.

exercise.prompt: Match each description to the component.

items.text: Traps soot; needs regeneration and periodic ash cleaning
items.why: The particulate filter collects soot.

items.text: Uses a urea solution to convert NOx into nitrogen and water
items.why: SCR relies on DEF.

items.text: Oxidizes CO and hydrocarbons, and creates heat that helps regeneration
items.why: The oxidation catalyst sits upstream of the DPF.

items.text: A differential pressure sensor measures how loaded it is
items.why: Pressure difference across the filter indicates loading.

check.q: Which duty cycle makes DPF loading problems more likely?
o: Heavy idling and short, stop-and-go trips
check.e: Low exhaust temperatures limit passive regeneration.

check.q: DEF can freeze in cold weather, which is why DEF tanks and lines are heated.
check.e: DEF freezes around 12 °F (−11 °C). Systems are designed to thaw it.

takeaways: Exhaust path: engine → DOC → DPF → DEF dosing → SCR → stack.
Regeneration can be passive, active or parked.
DEF is 32.5% urea and freezes around 12 °F.
Repeat DPF loading means an upstream cause still exists.
tips: Ask "When did the truck last complete a regen?" on DPF calls.
Ask for idle percentage from telematics on repeat offenders.
mistakes: Sending an aftertreatment derate to a shop without the right diagnostic software.
Assuming every HEST lamp is a fault.

blocks.title: Questions for any DPF / DEF call

objectives: Break down an estimate into its components
Understand labor hours, rates and diagnostic fees
Recognize common fees and core charges
body: An estimate is the shop's projected cost for a repair. Reading it well is one of the most valuable skills a coordinator can have.

head: Line
Description
Amount
rows: Refundable when old pump is returned

accordion.title: Labor and shop rates
accordion.text: Labor = hours × shop rate. Many shops use published "book" times for standard jobs. Rates vary by region and shop type — dealers often charge more than independents; roadside and after-hours work often carries premiums.

accordion.title: Diagnostics
accordion.text: Diagnostic time is billed separately from the repair. It is legitimate — finding the cause takes time and equipment — but it should be reasonable and not duplicated.

accordion.title: Parts
accordion.text: Check part prices against typical pricing. Ask whether parts are new, remanufactured or used, and about warranty.

accordion.title: Core charges
accordion.text: A [[Core]] charge is a deposit on a rebuildable part (starters, alternators, turbochargers, etc.). It is refunded when the old part is returned in acceptable condition. Make sure cores are returned — unreturned cores are lost money.

accordion.title: Fees
accordion.text: Shop supplies, environmental/disposal fees, service call or mileage charges for mobile work, and taxes. Know which your vendors charge and whether they are reasonable.

example.title: The duplicate diagnosis
example.text: A truck towed from Shop A to Shop B arrived with a diagnosis already completed. Shop B's estimate included 2.0 h of diagnostics. The coordinator asked why; Shop B agreed to verify the prior diagnosis in 0.5 h instead — saving 1.5 h of labor.

exercise.source:
Labor: 2.0 h @ $170/h
Alternator (reman): $410.00
Core charge: $120.00 (refundable)
Shop supplies: $25.00
Mobile service call: $150.00

check.q: What is a core charge?
o: A deposit refunded when the old rebuildable part is returned
A charge for engine work only
check.e: Core charges encourage return of rebuildable parts; return the core to get the refund.

check.q: Labor of 3.5 hours at $185/hour equals:

takeaways: Estimates: diagnostics, labor, parts, cores, supplies, fees, taxes.
Labor = hours × rate; book times are common references.
Return cores to recover deposits.
Question duplicated or unusual charges politely.
tips: Check labor hours against book time for common jobs.
Track core returns until the credit shows up.
mistakes: Paying diagnostics twice when a unit moves between shops.
Treating the core charge as a cost instead of a deposit.

blocks.title: Example hourly labor rates by vendor type
blocks.note: Illustrative only — rates vary widely by region. Always compare total cost, not rate alone.

deep.title: Book vs actual
blocks: Book time is the published standard. Actual time can be higher (seized bolts, extra damage) or the shop may bill book regardless. Ask shops how they bill — and ask for an explanation when actual hours exceed book by a wide margin.

deep.title: Checking the final invoice
blocks: The estimate is what you approved. The invoice is what the shop wants paid. Compare them line by line before anyone pays, while the details are still fresh.

head: Line · T-118 brake job
Approved estimate
Invoice
Check
rows: Ask why 1.5 h over. Was extra time approved?
Brake shoes and drums, drive axles
Who approved it, and when? Ask for the measurement that failed.
Rate changed. Ask for the shop's policy.
Fine, if the old shoes went back. Make sure the credit posts.

ul: Same unit, VIN and odometer as the case.
Every line is on the approved estimate or has a recorded approval.
Labor hours match the estimate or book time, or there is a reason.
Parts prices match the quote; warranty items are not billed to you.
Shop supplies and fees follow the agreed policy.
Cores are returned and their credits tracked.

exercise.prompt: Which T-118 invoice lines do you question before approving payment?

options.text: Labor billed at 5.5 hours
options.why: 1.5 hours over the approved estimate with no recorded approval.

options.text: Brake shoes and drums
options.why: Matches the estimate exactly.

options.text: Two slack adjusters
options.why: Not on the estimate. Unapproved work needs an explanation before payment.

options.text: Shop supplies at 15%
options.why: The rate is higher than the estimate used. Ask for the policy.

options.text: Brake shoe core charge
options.why: It was on the estimate and is refunded when the cores are accepted.

objectives: Handle additional repair recommendations
Follow approval procedures
Identify potential warranty coverage
body: Shops often find more than the original complaint. Some findings are safety-critical; some are recommendations that can wait. Your job is to sort them — with the technician's input — and route approvals correctly.

head: Finding type
Example
Typical handling
rows: Brake lining below minimum, leaking air chamber
Must be fixed before release; route approval quickly
Hose damaged while replacing water pump
Usually approve with the main repair
Wiper blades worn, minor oil seep
Defer to next PM if safe; document
Replace all belts "while we're in there" at low mileage

body: Most companies set approval limits: coordinators may approve up to a certain amount; above that, a fleet manager must approve. Document every approval — who, when, how much — and issue a PO if your company uses them.

[[Warranty]] may apply to new vehicles (base warranty), extended warranties on specific components, and parts/labor warranties on previous repairs. Before approving a repair, check: vehicle age and mileage, component warranty terms, and whether this part was replaced recently.

callout.title: Ask before work starts
callout.text: Warranty claims are much easier when identified before the repair. Some warranty repairs must be done at authorized dealers; a non-authorized shop could void the claim.

body.title: Example approval path by amount
body.note: Limits differ in every company. Never split an invoice to fit under a limit.

example.title: The upsell
example.text: An estimate for a starter replacement came back with batteries, cables, alternator and belts added — tripling the cost. The coordinator asked for test results. Batteries tested weak (legitimate), cables were fine, the alternator tested within spec. Approved: starter + batteries. Deferred: the rest, documented for the next PM.

exercise.prompt: Original complaint: trailer brake light out. Which items should you question or verify before approving? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Replace brake light lamp — $38
options.why: This addresses the complaint.

options.text: Replace all trailer tires — $2,480 (no measurements provided)
options.why: Unrelated and no evidence provided — ask for tread depths/photos.

options.text: Diagnostic fee 2.0 h for a light bulb
options.why: Excessive diagnostic time for a simple lighting issue — question it.

options.text: Repair corroded pigtail connector found at the light — $65
options.why: Related to the complaint and likely the cause.

options.text: Service call fee — $150 (mobile)
options.why: Normal for mobile service.

check.q: An estimate exceeds your approval limit. You should:
o: Route to the fleet manager per procedure with a clear summary
Ask the shop to split the invoice
Delay until the shop lowers it
check.e: Follow approval procedure. Never split invoices to avoid limits.

check.q: Warranty should be checked before the repair starts whenever possible.
check.e: Identifying warranty early avoids voiding claims and paying for covered work.

takeaways: Sort additional findings: safety-critical, related, recommended, questionable.
Ask for evidence on large or unrelated additions.
Follow approval limits and document approvals.
Check warranty before work begins.
tips: Ask for photos or measurements on any "recommended" item.
Check warranty before anyone picks up a wrench.
mistakes: Approving "while we're in there" work with no evidence.
Letting a non-authorized shop do warranty-eligible work.

blocks.title: From $6,800 requested to $2,040 approved
blocks.note: Starter + batteries (which tested weak) approved. Deferred items documented for the next PM.

objectives: Compare vendor types
Evaluate shop capabilities and availability
Weigh price, speed and quality

tiles.title: In-house shop
tiles.text: Company-owned. Lowest cost and full control — but only where you have terminals.

tiles.title: Dealer
tiles.text: Brand-specific expertise, factory tools, warranty authority. Often higher rates and longer waits.

tiles.title: Independent shop
tiles.text: Often faster and cheaper for general repairs. Capabilities vary widely.

tiles.title: Mobile service
tiles.text: Comes to the unit — tires, minor repairs, some diagnostics. No lift or heavy equipment.

tiles.title: Towing
tiles.text: Moves disabled units. Heavy-duty wreckers are needed for loaded tractor-trailers.

tiles.title: Tire networks
tiles.text: 24/7 roadside tire service across wide areas.

ol: Capability — Can you work on this make, system and problem? Do you have the diagnostic software?
Availability — When can you look at it? How many units are ahead?
Parts — Do you stock or can you get the likely parts quickly?
Pricing — Labor rate, diagnostic fee, after-hours premiums?
Communication — Who is my contact and when will I hear the diagnosis?

callout.title: Closest is not always fastest
callout.text: A shop 10 miles away with a 3-day backlog is slower than one 45 miles away that can start today. Factor in tow cost, but compare total downtime.

body.title: Closest isn't fastest: hours until work starts
body.note: Example comparison. Add tow cost and parts availability before deciding.

example.title: Dealer vs independent
example.text: T-118 needs a warranty-eligible emissions repair. The independent shop can start today; the dealer can start tomorrow. Because warranty work generally requires an authorized dealer, the coordinator chooses the dealer — saving the company the full repair cost for one extra day of downtime, and informs dispatch.

exercise.prompt: Loaded tractor-trailer, engine failure, cannot move, on I-40. Tractor is out of warranty. Which option?

options.text: Mobile mechanic to attempt engine repair on the shoulder
options.why: Major engine failures need a shop; the shoulder is unsafe for long repairs.

options.text: Heavy-duty tow to an independent shop 30 miles away that can diagnose today, plus a recovery tractor for the loaded trailer
options.why: Gets the unit to a capable shop quickly and protects the load separately.

options.text: Tell the driver to wait until the dealer 200 miles away has an opening next week
options.why: Unacceptable downtime and the driver is stranded.

check.q: Which vendor type typically has warranty authority for a manufacturer?
check.e: Authorized dealers typically perform warranty repairs.

check.q: The nearest shop is always the best choice.
check.e: Availability, capability and parts often matter more than distance.

takeaways: Know the strengths of each vendor type.
Ask about capability, availability, parts, pricing and communication.
Compare total downtime, not just distance.
Warranty work generally requires an authorized facility.
tips: Ask "when can you actually start?" — not "are you open?"
Confirm the shop has the diagnostic software for that engine make.
mistakes: Choosing a shop only because it's closest.
Not asking about parts availability until after diagnosis.

blocks.title: Choosing a vendor type
blocks.hint: General tendencies. Your best vendors may break the pattern — measure them.

objectives: Know when mobile service is appropriate
Order the right type of tow
Build a vendor network across your routes

no.title: Usually needs a shop
items: Work requiring a lift or heavy tools
Anything unsafe to perform on a roadside

body: Give the tow company: exact location and direction of travel, unit type (tractor only, or tractor + loaded trailer), approximate weight, what's wrong (won't start, no brakes release, collision), destination shop, and billing information. Heavy-duty wreckers are required for tractors; loaded combinations may need special equipment.

callout.title: Tow costs add up
callout.text: Towing is often billed by hookup, mileage, and hourly time. A long tow to a preferred shop can cost more than the repair difference. Compare total cost.

body: Map your fleet's common lanes and build a list of trusted vendors along each: shops, tire services, mobile mechanics and towers — with hours, capabilities and contacts. When a call comes in at 02:00, a prepared list saves precious time.

body.title: Tow order checklist
rows: I-30 WB, mile marker 118, right shoulder
Brakes won't release after air loss

example.title: The prepared lane
example.text: A fleet running Dallas–Atlanta keeps a vendor list for each 150-mile segment of I-20. When T-133 blew a steer tire near Meridian, MS at 01:30, the coordinator had a 24-hour tire service on the phone in two minutes.

practical.title: What does the tow company need?

exercise.prompt: Select all the information you should give when ordering a tow.

options.text: Exact location and direction of travel
options.why: The wrecker must find the unit safely.

options.text: Tractor only or tractor with loaded trailer
options.why: Determines wrecker type and equipment.

options.text: The driver's home address
options.why: Not relevant — and personal information should not be shared unnecessarily.

options.text: Destination shop
options.why: Needed to quote and plan.

options.text: Nature of the problem (e.g., brakes won't release)
options.why: Affects how the unit can be towed.

options.text: Billing / PO information
options.why: Prevents delays and payment disputes.

check.q: Which job is best suited to mobile service?
check.e: Tire replacement is routine for mobile tire services.

check.q: Tow costs can exceed the savings of using a preferred shop far away.
check.e: Compare total cost including tow and downtime.

takeaways: Mobile service fits light, on-site repairs.
Give tow companies complete, precise information.
Compare total cost including tow and downtime.
Build vendor lists along your lanes before you need them.
tips: Keep a lane-by-lane vendor list with after-hours numbers.
Ask tow companies for hookup, mileage and hourly rates before dispatching.
mistakes: Ordering a light-duty wrecker for a tractor.
Towing 150 miles to a preferred shop when a capable one is 30 miles away.

blocks.title: Match the wrecker to the job
head: Type
Typical use
rows: Cars and light pickups — not for tractors
Box trucks and smaller commercial vehicles
Recovery after rollovers or off-road incidents
Hauling equipment that can't be towed on its wheels

deep.title: Ordering a heavy tow
blocks: A tow ordered with missing details arrives with the wrong truck, or not at all. Give the tow company everything in one call.

head: Tell them
Why it matters
rows: Unit and combination: tractor only, or tractor and trailer; loaded or empty; rough weight
Decides the wrecker class and whether the trailer goes too
Exact location: road, direction, exit or mile marker, shoulder or lane, a GPS pin
The wrecker finds the truck the first time
What is wrong: no-start, brakes locked, air leak, crash damage
Locked spring brakes need air supplied or the brakes caged before the truck can roll
Destination: shop name, address, hours, and that they will accept it
Avoids a tow to a closed gate
Payment: quoted rate (hook-up plus per mile, or hourly), PO number, who signs

callout.title: The driveline question
callout.text: Towing a tractor with its drive wheels on the ground usually means disconnecting the driveshaft or pulling the axle shafts, so the transmission is not damaged. The operator knows this; make sure it is in the quote and on the invoice.

callout.title: Get it in writing
callout.text: Get the ETA and the quote by text or email before you confirm. Then give the driver the tow company's name and ETA.

deep.title: Reading a roadside service ticket
blocks: Roadside work is billed differently from shop work: a call-out fee, mileage to reach the truck, roadside labor rates and sometimes a parts run. Check each one against what you authorized.

blocks.text: Loud air leak and low-air warning, right rear drive axle.
Replaced right rear drive spring brake chamber (type 30/30). Adjusted; brakes tested and released.

notes.d: Response time is call to on-site: 90 minutes here. Repair time on site: 1 h 35 min.
Should match where the truck was. It also explains the mileage.
A flat fee for coming out. Often higher at night and on weekends.
Usually round trip from the vendor's base. Check that the distance makes sense.
Higher than shop rates, often with a one-hour minimum.
A charge for fetching a part the truck did not carry. It should match what you approved.
The exact part fitted. Note it for warranty.
$1,040.25 against a $1,200 authorization: OK. Anything over needs approval first.
Technician and driver. Keep the ticket with the case.

exercise.source: Call received 14:35 · On site 16:05 · Mileage 64 mi round trip · Total due $1,040.25 · Authorized up to $1,200

objectives: Identify tire positions on a tractor-trailer
Recognize common wear patterns and what they suggest
Give a tire vendor everything they need
body: Tires are one of the largest maintenance costs in a fleet and one of the most common roadside calls. Precise position information gets the right tire to the right place the first time.

body.title: Tire and roadside numbers to know (U.S.)

items.l: tires on a standard five-axle tractor-trailer
minimum tread depth on other positions
to place warning devices after a stop on the road

body.note: Based on FMCSA rules (49 CFR 393.75 and 392.22). Your safety department is the authority on how they apply.

body.h: Wear patterns and what they suggest

tiles.title: Center wear
tiles.text: Often linked to over-inflation.

tiles.title: Both shoulders worn
tiles.text: Often linked to under-inflation.

tiles.title: One-side / feathered wear
tiles.text: Often points to alignment (toe or camber) problems.

tiles.title: Cupping / scalloping
tiles.text: Can suggest suspension, balance or bearing issues.

tiles.title: Flat spot
tiles.text: Often from a brake lock-up or skid.

tiles.title: Bulge or exposed cords
tiles.text: Internal damage — replace; a blowout risk.

body: Wear patterns are clues for a technician, not a diagnosis. Their value to you: a tire that wore out early usually means another cost (alignment, suspension, inflation) is still waiting to be fixed.

ul: Unit and exact location
Position: axle, side, inside or outside dual
Tire size (on the sidewall, e.g. 295/75R22.5 or 11R22.5)
Wheel damage? (steel or aluminum wheel)
Is the vehicle loaded?
Billing / PO and any fleet tire program

body.title: Same depth, different verdict: tread depth by position
body.note: U.S. minimums under 49 CFR 393.75: 4/32 in for steer tires, 2/32 in for all other positions. 3/32 in is legal on a drive tire but not on a steer tire. Many fleets replace tires well before the legal minimum by policy.

body.title: Duals vs wide-base singles

items.sub: Two tires on each end of a drive or trailer axle.
facts: If one fails, the wheel end isn't left bare — but the partner is suddenly overloaded
Both tires must be matched in size and wear to share the load
items.watch: An underinflated inner dual overloads the outer one. After a flat, have the partner inspected too.

items.sub: One wide tire replaces each pair of duals (for example, 445/50R22.5).
facts: No partner tire — a failure leaves that wheel end with nothing
items.watch: Roadside stock is thinner in some areas. Keep your fleet's wide-base sizes in the tire vendor list.

body.key: With duals, the partner tire takes the whole load when one fails and must be inspected too; with a wide-base single there is no partner at all. Either way, the driver stops safely and a tire technician decides whether the unit can move.

body.h: Leaks and low pressure: the most common out-of-service tire call

body: Tread depth gets the attention, but a leaking or under-inflated tire is the single most common vehicle out-of-service violation in recent FMCSA data. A tire run low builds heat, damages its casing and can fail at speed, often taking its dual partner with it.

head: What the driver reports
What it means
What you do
rows: Flat, or a hiss you can hear
Unit stays parked. Send mobile tire service with axle, side and position.
Gauge reading under half of the pressure on the sidewall
Recorded as out of service at roadside
Same as a flat: send service to the unit.
A few psi low, no hiss
Too low for the load is still a violation (49 CFR 393.75(h))
Have it aired up and checked for a slow leak at the next safe stop or shop.
A real leak until proven otherwise
Ask for a gauge reading on that tire and its dual partner.

callout.title: Ask for the number
callout.text: Ask the driver for the pressure reading and the pressure molded on the sidewall. "It looks a little low" is not enough to decide whether the truck can move.

example.title: The hidden inner dual
example.text: A driver reported "a tire looks low" on the right side of drive axle 2. The coordinator asked which dual. The outer looked fine — the inner was nearly flat and had been overloading its partner for miles. The tire service replaced both after inspection found the outer had been damaged by overheating.

exercise.source:
Unit T-133 with TR-518. I-20 EB near mile marker 42.
Trailer, rear axle, left side, outside tire — tread came off, wheel looks OK.
Tire says 295/75R22.5. Loaded.

check.q: Wear on both shoulders of a tire most often suggests:
check.e: Under-inflated tires carry load on the shoulders.

check.q: Why ask "inside or outside dual?"
o: The vendor needs exact position, and an inside flat can overload the outside tire
check.e: Position precision saves time and prevents a second failure.

check.q: A driver hears a steady hiss from a trailer tire at a fuel stop. What is the right call?
o: Drive to the shop 15 miles away before it gets worse
Keep the unit parked and send mobile tire service with the exact position
Air it up and keep going to the delivery
check.e: A tire with an audible leak is out of service (49 CFR 393.75(a)(3)). Send service to the unit with axle, side and inside/outside position.

check.q: On work order 7731-0442, why was the right steer tire replaced?
o: It was more than 2 years old
Its tread was 3/32 in, below the 4/32 in steer minimum
check.e: Steer tires need at least 4/32 in of tread under 49 CFR 393.75.

check.q: A tire's DOT code ends in 1921. When was it made?
check.e: The last four digits are the week and year of manufacture.

takeaways: A standard tractor-trailer has 18 tires: 2 steer, 8 drive, 8 trailer.
Steer tires need at least 4/32″ tread; other positions 2/32″ (U.S.).
Wear patterns point to other problems to fix.
Give vendors axle, side, dual position, size and location.
tips: Ask drivers to photograph the sidewall size when safe.
Track tire failures by position — patterns point to alignment or inflation issues.
After any wheel comes off, ask the vendor to re-check lug-nut torque after the first 50–100 miles, as most wheel makers recommend. Loose wheels can come off.
mistakes: "Left rear tire" on an 18-wheeler — there are eight rear tires on the left.
Replacing a worn tire without asking why it wore early.

deep.title: Reading a tire service work order
blocks: A tire shop's work order records every position it touched, with tread depth, pressure and the tire's age. Read it to confirm the right tires were changed, the law was met and nothing was missed.

cells: Slow leak at valve: core replaced, aired to 100 psi
Flat, casing damaged: replaced with retread

notes.d: Axle, side, and inner or outer on duals. It must match what the driver reported.
Steer tires need at least 4/32 in of tread, other positions 2/32 in (49 CFR 393.75). 3/32 on a steer is replaced, not watched.
72 psi against 100 on its partner means a leak. Low pressure ruins casings and causes blowouts.
The last four digits of the DOT code on the sidewall are the week and year the tire was made: 3122 means week 31 of 2022. The shop copies it to this column. Old tires are worth flagging.
Retreads are common on trailers and drives. A damaged old tire may earn a smaller credit, or none.
When one dual goes flat, its partner carried double load. Check it.
Record the torque and plan a re-check after the first 50–100 miles.
Tires, mounting, balancing, small parts, disposal, minus credits, plus tax.

objectives: Break total downtime into stages
Identify which stages the coordinator controls
Measure downtime consistently
body: [[Downtime]] is the time a unit is unavailable for work because of maintenance. Total downtime is made of stages — and each stage has different levers.

head: Stage
Typical driver of delay
Coordinator lever
rows: Send complete complaint details and history
Source alternatives; expedite; check other suppliers
Limited — but prioritize and confirm ETR

callout.title: Invisible downtime
callout.text: Approval waits and pickup waits are often the easiest hours to eliminate — and they are 100% within the coordinator's control.

body.title: The timestamps that measure downtime
body.note: Record every timestamp on every case. The gap between any two of them is a stage you can measure — and compare across vendors, terminals and months.

example.title: Where did 31 hours go?
example.text: T-108 was down 31 hours. Breakdown: 2 h tow, 9 h waiting for the shop to start, 2 h diagnosis, 11 h waiting for approval overnight, 1 h parts, 4 h repair, 2 h waiting for a driver. Only 7 hours were actual work. The coordinator's review led to after-hours approval coverage.

exercise.prompt: In the T-108 example, which stages were most within the coordinator's control? (Select all that apply)

options.text: 11 h waiting for approval
options.why: Routing approvals and after-hours coverage are process issues.

options.text: 4 h repair time
options.why: Actual repair time depends on the job.

options.text: 2 h waiting for a driver after release
options.why: Coordinating pickup with dispatch before release eliminates this.

options.text: 9 h waiting for shop to start
options.why: Choosing a shop with capacity is a coordinator decision.

check.q: Which downtime stage is usually most within the coordinator's control?
check.e: Approvals are a process the coordinator drives directly.

check.q: Downtime only counts the hours a technician is working on the unit.
check.e: Downtime covers the full period the unit is unavailable.

takeaways: Downtime = all time the unit is unavailable.
Break it into stages to find delays.
Approval and pickup waits are controllable.
Measure consistently from down to returned to service.

objectives: Build realistic ETRs
Communicate confidence levels
Apply tactics that shorten downtime
body: An [[ETR]] is only useful if people can plan around it. Build it from the stages, not from hope.

head: Confidence
When
How to say it
rows: "ETR tomorrow 10:00 if the part arrives on the 07:00 delivery."
"No ETR until diagnosis — expected by 13:00. Plan for at least tomorrow."

ul: Approve quickly when within limits; escalate fast when not
Ask the shop to order parts during diagnosis if likely
Source parts from alternate suppliers or dealers
Pre-arrange the driver pickup for release time
Ask whether safe, non-critical repairs can be deferred to the next PM

body.title: Building an ETR from its stages
body.note: Approval runs in parallel with shipping, so the part — not the approval — sets the ETR.

body.title: How confident is this ETR?

stops.d: Before diagnosis — a range, not a time.
Diagnosed; parts identified but not in hand.

body.note: Say the confidence level with every ETR: "Likely 16:00 — parts arrive at 13:00." Dispatch plans differently for each level.

example.title: Parts from 60 miles away
example.text: The shop's parts supplier quoted two days for a turbo actuator. The coordinator called three other suppliers; one had it 60 miles away. A courier delivered it the same afternoon for $140 — cheaper than one more day of downtime.

exercise.prompt: Diagnosis done 10:00. Approval takes 30 min. Part arrives 13:00. Repair is 3 h, road test 30 min. Best ETR?

options.why: Ignores repair and road test time.
Work starts when the part arrives at 13:00 (approval is done by then): 13:00 + 3 h + 0.5 h = 16:30.
Too optimistic.

check.q: Diagnosis isn't complete. What's the best way to communicate the ETR?
o: Say there is no ETR yet, when diagnosis is expected, and a planning assumption
check.e: Honest, with a time for the next update and a planning assumption.

check.q: A courier fee can be justified if it saves a day of downtime.
check.e: Compare the fee to the cost of downtime.

takeaways: Build ETRs from stages.
State confidence: high, medium, low.
Parallelize: order likely parts during diagnosis.
Spending a little can save a lot of downtime.
tips: Find the critical path — the longest chain of steps that can't overlap.
Ask shops to order likely parts during diagnosis.
mistakes: Adding every stage end-to-end when some run in parallel.
Giving an ETR without saying how confident you are.

objectives: Explain the impact of maintenance on pickups and deliveries
Account for driver hours of service
Understand deadhead costs
body: Every maintenance decision is also an operations decision. When a truck is down, a load, a driver, and a customer are affected.

tiles.title: Loads
tiles.text: A loaded trailer may be stuck with a broken tractor, or a load may need to be reassigned.

tiles.title: Appointments
tiles.text: Pickup and delivery windows can be tight. Missing them may cost fees, rescheduling, or customer trust.

tiles.title: Driver schedules
tiles.text: Drivers have home-time plans and limited hours; a long repair may cost them a day.

tiles.title: Deadhead
tiles.text: Miles driven empty (no revenue) — e.g., sending a truck to recover a load or to a shop.

body: U.S. property-carrying drivers must follow [[HOS]] rules — for example, a limit of 11 hours driving within a 14-hour on-duty window after 10 consecutive hours off, among other limits. Time spent waiting at a shop can count against the driver's on-duty window depending on how it is logged. A 6-hour repair might leave the driver unable to finish the trip legally. Dispatch and safety manage HOS; your ETRs are what they plan with.

callout.title: Always ask dispatch
callout.text: Before choosing between a fast-but-far shop and a slow-but-near shop, ask dispatch what matters most for this load: time, location, or the driver's hours.

body.title: The 14-hour trap
body.note: Simplified example of the U.S. 14-hour on-duty window. Dispatch and safety own hours-of-service decisions — your accurate ETR is what they plan with.

body.title: Recovery options when a loaded unit goes down
head: Option
When it fits
Trade-off
rows: Short, reliable ETR; delivery window still reachable
All risk sits on one ETR
Tractor is down, trailer is fine, another tractor is nearby
Deadhead miles and a second driver's time
Truck will be fixed, but the driver is out of hours
Needs a rested driver near the shop
Customer can accept a later time
Trailer itself can't move (or a straight truck is down)
body.note: Dispatch chooses — your job is to give a realistic ETR early enough that every option is still open.

example.title: The 14-hour trap
example.text: A driver started at 06:00. At 11:00 the truck broke down. The repair finished at 16:30. With the 14-hour window ending at 20:00, the driver had 3.5 hours left — not enough to reach a delivery 5 hours away. Knowing this, dispatch arranged a relay with a fresh driver.

exercise.prompt: A loaded truck will be down 8 hours. Which pieces of information help dispatch plan? (Select all that apply)

options.text: ETR and confidence level
options.why: Timing is the core planning input.

options.text: Unit location and whether the trailer can be picked up by another tractor
options.why: Enables recovery options.

options.text: The shop's labor rate
options.why: Cost matters to maintenance, not dispatch's load plan.

options.text: Whether the driver can wait in the shop lounge or needs a hotel
options.why: Affects driver care and HOS planning.

check.q: What is deadhead?
o: Miles driven with no revenue load
check.e: Deadhead miles are empty, non-revenue miles.

check.q: A long repair can prevent a driver from legally finishing a trip even after the truck is fixed.
check.e: Hours-of-service limits may run out during downtime.

takeaways: Maintenance decisions affect loads, appointments, drivers and customers.
HOS limits can turn a repair delay into a missed delivery.
Deadhead adds cost without revenue.
Ask dispatch what matters most for each load.
tips: Tell dispatch early when a repair will eat into the driver's day.
Ask whether a relay driver is possible before the repair finishes.
mistakes: Assuming a fixed truck means an on-time load.
Pressuring a driver to "push through" after a long repair.

yes.title: Drop & hook
items: Driver drops a trailer and picks up another
A down tractor can often be replaced easily

no.title: Live load / unload
items: Delays ripple into the driver's hours

objectives: Evaluate recovery options for a stranded load
Decide when to swap equipment
Coordinate replacement equipment

head: Option
When it makes sense
Trade-offs
rows: Lowest cost, but risk if ETR slips
Another tractor picks up the trailer — deadhead miles, needs available driver
Trailer down, cargo can be transloaded
Labor and time to transfer cargo

body: Your role: give dispatch accurate facts (ETR, confidence, location, whether trailer is mobile) so they can choose. Often you also coordinate the logistics — where the swap happens, keys, paperwork, and the broken unit's path to repair.

callout.title: Decide early
callout.text: The later a recovery decision is made, the fewer options remain. If the ETR confidence is low, raise the recovery conversation early.

example.title: Power swap in Little Rock
example.text: T-118 broke down with a time-sensitive load. The ETR was tomorrow afternoon. T-140 was empty 50 miles away. Dispatch sent T-140 to pick up the trailer; the coordinator arranged the shop to release the trailer, and T-118 stayed for repair. The load arrived on time.

exercise.prompt: Tractor down, ETR 30+ hours (parts). Loaded trailer is fine. Delivery tomorrow 08:00, 300 miles away. An empty tractor is 40 miles away. Best plan?

options.text: Wait for the repair
options.why: Guarantees a missed delivery.

options.text: Power swap: send the empty tractor to take the trailer; keep the broken tractor at the shop
options.why: Protects the delivery with minimal deadhead.

options.text: Transload the cargo to another trailer
options.why: The trailer is fine — transloading adds labor and time for no reason.

check.q: A trailer is damaged and cannot move, but the cargo is intact. Best option is usually:
check.e: The cargo must move to a working trailer.

check.q: Recovery decisions are best made as late as possible.
check.e: Early decisions preserve more options.

takeaways: Options: wait, power swap, trailer swap, rental, reschedule.
Give dispatch facts early so they can choose.
Coordinate swap logistics and the broken unit's repair path.
Low ETR confidence = raise recovery early.
tips: Raise the recovery conversation when ETR confidence drops — not when the ETR is missed.
Coordinate keys, paperwork and swap location yourself.
mistakes: Transloading cargo when the trailer is fine.
Waiting on a low-confidence ETR with a firm delivery.

objectives: List the key fleet tracking data points
Explain how each supports decisions
Recognize early warning signs in fleet data

head: Track
Why it matters
rows: Know what's available and what's down
Drive PM scheduling and warranty checks
Detect root-cause problems and warranty claims

callout.title: Early warning signs
callout.text: Same unit with the same complaint twice in 30 days. A vendor whose repairs keep coming back. PM compliance dropping. Downtime rising while repair counts are flat (a process problem). These patterns deserve attention before they become crises.

body: The next lesson puts this into practice with an interactive fleet board.

body.title: Downtime hours by system — one month
body.note: When one bar dominates, look for a small number of units driving it — here, one tractor logged 64 h.

industry.name: Samsara
industry.text: Samsara offers a connected operations platform. Its website lists fleet capabilities including live GPS tracking, vehicle diagnostics, fuel analytics and compliance reporting, plus AI-powered dash cams and in-cab alerts for driver safety.
industry.relevance: Telematics platforms supply several data points on this list — location, diagnostics and fault codes — so coordinators can track units without waiting for a phone call.

body.title: Early warning signs in fleet data
head: What you see
What it can mean
rows: Same unit, same system, twice in 90 days
Repeat failure — the root cause wasn't fixed
PMs slipping past due on one terminal
Capacity or scheduling problem at that location
One vendor's repairs keep coming back
Quality issue — review comebacks with the vendor
Fuel economy dropping on one unit
Tires, brakes or engine issue worth inspecting
Downtime rising while repair costs stay flat
Time is lost waiting — approvals, parts or pickup

example.title: Spotting the repeat
example.text: During weekly review the coordinator notices T-120 has three aftertreatment cases in 60 days at two different shops. Individually each looked routine. Together they point to an unresolved root cause — and possibly warranty coverage on the first repair.

exercise.prompt: Which of these deserve follow-up? (Select all that apply)

options.text: T-120: DPF-related repairs on 04/02, 04/28, 05/30
options.why: Repeat failure pattern.

options.text: T-131: One tire replaced after road debris
options.why: A one-off event with a clear external cause.

options.text: Vendor X: 4 of last 10 repairs returned within 30 days
options.why: Quality concern with the vendor.

options.text: PM compliance fell from 94% to 81% this month
options.why: Significant decline — find the cause.

check.q: Downtime is rising while the number of repairs is flat. This most likely indicates:
o: A process problem such as slow approvals, parts or shop backlog
check.e: Same work, more time = a process bottleneck.

check.q: A single tire replaced after road debris is a repeat-failure pattern.
check.e: Repeat patterns are the same problem recurring on a unit or with a vendor.

takeaways: Track status, mileage, PM, open repairs, downtime, repeats and vendors.
Each data point supports a specific decision.
Look for patterns, not just individual cases.
Rising downtime with flat repairs = process issue.
tips: Sort by downtime and by repeats every week.
Look at patterns across units, vendors and routes — not only single cases.
mistakes: Reviewing cases one by one and missing the pattern.
Tracking repairs but not downtime.

objectives: Navigate a fleet status dashboard
Filter and sort to find priorities
Turn dashboard data into actions
body: Use the interactive fleet board below. Filter by status, search units, sort columns, and open a unit to see its history. Then answer the knowledge check using what you find.

callout.title: Morning routine
callout.text: 1) Check units down and their ETRs. 2) Check overdue/due PMs. 3) Review repeat-failure flags. 4) Plan today's follow-ups.

industry.name: Fleetio
industry.text: Fleetio is fleet management software. Its website describes it as "one place to run fleet maintenance," aimed at reducing downtime and controlling costs, for fleets in industries including trucking and freight.
industry.relevance: Fleet maintenance software is where a fleet board like the one above usually lives in real operations — unit status, PM due dates and repair history in one place.

example.title: From data to action
example.text: Filtering the board to "Overdue" PM status shows two units. Sorting by downtime shows which in-shop units are hurting availability most. Opening a unit's history shows whether a repeat failure deserves a root-cause review. Each view becomes a to-do list.

ol: Filter to units that are not Active — note each unit's status and ETR.
Filter PM status to Overdue — which units need scheduling?
Sort by repeat failures — which unit needs a root-cause review?
Open that unit and read its history.

check.q: On the fleet board, which unit shows the highest number of repeat failures?
check.e: T-120 has repeated aftertreatment failures — a candidate for root-cause analysis.

check.q: What is the first thing to review each morning?
check.e: Down units affect today's operations the most.

takeaways: Filter and sort to find priorities fast.
Status, PM, repeats and downtime each produce a to-do list.
Open unit histories to understand patterns.
Build a consistent daily review routine.

blocks.title: Road calls by unit and month
blocks.note: Heatmaps make repeat offenders obvious at a glance. T-101 and T-120 deserve reviews.

objectives: Calculate maintenance cost per mile
Compare preventive and reactive maintenance costs
Identify the main cost drivers
body: [[CPM]] (cost per mile) normalizes spending so units and fleets can be compared: maintenance cost ÷ miles driven.

no.title: Reactive
items: Happens at the worst time and place
Missed loads, driver pay, customer impact

callout.title: The hidden multiplier
callout.text: A reactive repair usually costs more than the repair itself: tow, premiums, downtime, recovery and customer impact. That is why PM compliance is one of the strongest cost-control tools.

body.title: One year per tractor: PM-driven vs. reactive
body.note: Illustrative figures to show the pattern, not a benchmark.

example.title: Two tractors, same model
example.text: T-114: $9,800 over 120,000 miles = $0.082/mi. T-120: $18,600 over 110,000 miles = $0.169/mi. T-120 costs roughly twice as much per mile — and its history shows repeated aftertreatment repairs. CPM points you to where to look.

exercise.source:
Parts: $6,200
Labor: $4,900
Tires: $2,400
Other (tows, fees): $500
Miles driven: 125,000

check.q: Cost per mile is calculated as:
check.e: CPM = cost ÷ miles.

check.q: Reactive repairs often cost more than the repair invoice alone.
check.e: Tows, premiums, downtime and recovery add hidden costs.

takeaways: CPM = maintenance cost ÷ miles.
Use CPM to compare units and spot outliers.
Reactive maintenance carries hidden costs.
PM compliance is a primary cost-control lever.
tips: Compare CPM between similar units — outliers deserve a look.
Include tows and downtime when you talk about the cost of a failure.
mistakes: Cutting PM to save money this month.
Comparing CPM across very different duty cycles.

blocks.title: Why CPM rose from $0.118 to $0.131 (cents per mile)
blocks.note: Rounded example. A CPM bridge turns "costs went up" into specific causes you can act on.

objectives: Quantify the cost of downtime
Compare vendor options by total cost
Recognize the cost of repeat repairs
body: The cheapest invoice is not always the cheapest repair. Include downtime and the risk of the repair coming back.
A repair that fails again costs the second repair, a second round of downtime, possibly another tow, and lost confidence. Ask for parts and labor warranties on repairs, and track comebacks by vendor.

Compare vendors on total cost: labor rate × realistic hours, parts pricing, fees, tow distance, and expected downtime. A higher rate with faster turnaround and fewer comebacks is often the better deal.

body.title: Vendor A vs. B once downtime is counted

example.title: The cheap shop that wasn't
example.text: Shop A quoted $1,200 with a 3-day wait. Shop B quoted $1,550 and could finish today. With downtime valued at $800/day, Shop A's real cost was roughly $1,200 + $2,400 = $3,600 versus Shop B's $1,550 + $0 = $1,550.

exercise.prompt: Downtime costs $900/day. Vendor A: $2,000, done in 1 day. Vendor B: $1,500, done in 3 days. Which is cheaper in total?

options.text: Vendor A: $2,900 total
Vendor B: $1,500 total
options.why: Ignores three days of downtime ($2,700).

options.text: They are equal
options.why: A is $1,300 cheaper in total.

check.q: Which is part of the true cost of a repeat repair?
o: Second invoice, additional downtime, possible tow and lost confidence
check.e: Repeats multiply cost beyond the invoice.

check.q: The vendor with the lowest labor rate always produces the lowest total cost.
check.e: Hours, speed, comebacks, tow distance and downtime matter.

takeaways: Downtime has a real daily cost — use it in decisions.
Compare vendors on total cost, not rate alone.
Repeat repairs multiply costs.
Ask for and track repair warranties and comebacks.
tips: Use a downtime cost per day your fleet agrees on.
Track comebacks per vendor — a cheap repair that fails twice isn't cheap.
mistakes: Choosing on invoice alone.
Ignoring tow distance in vendor comparisons.

objectives: Compare OEM, aftermarket and remanufactured parts
Ask the right sourcing questions
Balance price, availability, quality and warranty
body: Parts delays are one of the biggest sources of downtime. Knowing your options — and the trade-offs — lets you find a part today instead of next week.

body.title: Part types compared
body.hint: More dots = better for the fleet. General tendencies — quality varies by brand and supplier.

accordion.title: OEM (original equipment manufacturer)
accordion.text: Made by or for the vehicle/component manufacturer. Best fit certainty and often required for warranty repairs. Usually the highest price.

accordion.title: Aftermarket
accordion.text: Made by other manufacturers to fit. Quality ranges from excellent to poor — stick with suppliers your fleet trusts.

accordion.title: Remanufactured (reman)
accordion.text: Used cores rebuilt to specification, often with a warranty. Common for starters, alternators, turbos, injectors and ECMs. Usually involves a core charge.

accordion.title: Used / salvage
accordion.text: Occasionally useful for hard-to-find items or older units. Limited or no warranty — confirm condition and get approval.

body.title: Parts request checklist
rows: Price · core charge · warranty · ETA · alternatives

example.title: Reman saves a day
example.text: The dealer quoted a new OEM turbo actuator in 3 days. A reman supplier had one in stock 40 miles away with a 12-month warranty and a core charge. With approval and a warranty check (the unit was out of engine warranty), the coordinator sourced the reman part — the truck was back the same evening.

exercise.prompt: Tractor under engine warranty needs an EGR valve. OEM part: 2 days. Aftermarket: in stock today, 30% cheaper. What do you do?

options.text: Install the aftermarket part today to save time and money
options.why: Non-OEM parts or non-authorized repairs can jeopardize a warranty claim — the fleet could pay for a covered repair.

options.text: Check the warranty terms with an authorized dealer first; if covered, go OEM under warranty and plan around the 2-day wait (e.g., power swap)
options.why: Protects the warranty and manages downtime separately.

options.text: Buy a used part from salvage
options.why: Worst option for a warranty unit.

check.q: Which part type typically involves a core charge?
check.e: Reman parts are rebuilt from returned cores — hence the deposit.

check.q: Aftermarket parts are always lower quality than OEM.
check.e: Quality varies by supplier; many are excellent. Trust and warranty matter.

takeaways: OEM: best fit and warranty-friendly, usually costliest.
Aftermarket: price and availability; quality varies.
Reman: rebuilt, warrantied, core charge.
Check vehicle warranty before choosing a non-OEM part.
tips: Keep 3–4 trusted parts suppliers per region with after-hours contacts.
Always ask "Is there an alternative in stock?"
mistakes: Choosing the cheapest part on a warranty unit.
Forgetting to return the core.

objectives: Decide which parts to stock
Calculate a reorder point
Track cores and prevent obsolete stock
body: Fleets with their own shops or yards often keep parts on hand. The goal: the right parts available when needed, without tying up cash in shelves full of parts nobody uses.

body.title: ABC analysis: a few parts drive most of the usage (example)
body.note: Share of annual usage value. Stock A items carefully and review them often; C items may be ordered as needed.

items.f: daily usage × lead time days + safety stock
annual parts cost used ÷ avg inventory value
requests filled from stock ÷ total requests

body.title: Reorder point: brake chambers at a terminal
body.note: When stock on the shelf drops to 4, reorder. Safety stock covers busy weeks and late deliveries.

ul: PM kits: filters, belts, common fluids
High-failure safety items: brake chambers, slack adjusters, lamps, air fittings, glad-hand seals
Fast-moving tires for your common sizes
Batteries before winter

callout.title: Cores are money on the shelf
callout.text: Track every core from removal to return. An unreturned core means paying full price for a reman part.

example.title: The out-of-stock chamber
example.text: A terminal shop ran out of brake chambers during a busy week and a tractor waited a day for a delivery. After setting a reorder point of 4 with 2 units of safety stock, the shop didn't run out again that year.

exercise.source:
Average usage: 3 per week (≈ 0.43 per day)
Supplier lead time: 7 days
Safety stock policy: 2 units

fields.label: Usage during lead time (round to whole units)

check.q: Reorder point is:
o: Daily usage × lead time + safety stock
check.e: Order when stock falls to the expected lead-time usage plus a buffer.

check.q: In ABC analysis, "A" items are a small share of part numbers that drive most usage value.
check.e: Focus attention where the value is.

takeaways: Stock what fails often and what stops trucks.
Reorder point = usage × lead time + safety stock.
ABC analysis focuses attention on high-value items.
Track cores to recover deposits.
tips: Build PM kits per unit type — faster PMs, fewer missing parts.
Review slow-moving stock twice a year.
mistakes: Stocking parts for units the fleet no longer runs.
No safety stock on safety-critical items.
